deck.title: Chemical Equilibria: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium

front_blocks.md: Define **reversible reaction**.

back_blocks.md: A **reversible reaction** is one in which the products can react to reform the original reactants. It is represented using two opposing half arrows: ⇌

cards.front_md: Define **reversible reaction**.
cards.back_md: A **reversible reaction** is one in which the products can react to reform the original reactants. It is represented using two opposing half arrows: ⇌

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are **constant**, but they are not necessarily equal to each other.

cards.back_md:

front_blocks.md: What two conditions must be met for a dynamic equilibrium to exist?

back_blocks.md: A dynamic equilibrium requires: (1) the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction, and (2) the system is **closed** so no reactants or products can escape.

cards.front_md: What two conditions must be met for a dynamic equilibrium to exist?
cards.back_md: A dynamic equilibrium requires: (1) the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction, and (2) the system is **closed** so no reactants or products can escape.

front_blocks.md: In a dynamic equilibrium, the **..........**  of the forward reaction equals the **..........**  of the backward reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain **..........** .

back_blocks.md: In a dynamic equilibrium, the **rate** of the forward reaction equals the **rate** of the backward reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain **constant**.

cards.back_md: In a dynamic equilibrium, the **rate** of the forward reaction equals the **rate** of the backward reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain **constant**.

front_blocks.md: Define **closed system**.

back_blocks.md: A **closed system** is one in which none of the reactants or products can escape from the reaction mixture, allowing dynamic equilibrium to be established.

cards.front_md: Define **closed system**.
cards.back_md: A **closed system** is one in which none of the reactants or products can escape from the reaction mixture, allowing dynamic equilibrium to be established.

front_blocks.md: Why can a gas-phase equilibrium only be reached in a closed system?

back_blocks.md: In an **open system**, gaseous products escape to the surroundings, so the backward reaction cannot occur at the same rate as the forward reaction and **equilibrium is never established**.

cards.front_md: Why can a gas-phase equilibrium only be reached in a closed system?
cards.back_md: In an **open system**, gaseous products escape to the surroundings, so the backward reaction cannot occur at the same rate as the forward reaction and **equilibrium is never established**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In a dynamic equilibrium, reactant and product molecules are still reacting with each other.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The system is **dynamic** because forward and backward reactions continue to occur. Equilibrium means the rates are equal, not that the reactions have stopped.

front_blocks.md: What happens to the concentrations of reactants and products as a reaction approaches equilibrium from the reactants side?

back_blocks.md: The concentration of reactants **decreases** and the concentration of products **increases** until both become constant at equilibrium.

cards.front_md: What happens to the concentrations of reactants and products as a reaction approaches equilibrium from the reactants side?
cards.back_md: The concentration of reactants **decreases** and the concentration of products **increases** until both become constant at equilibrium.

front_blocks.md: A reaction that goes to completion uses up all the **..........**  and stops, whereas a **..........**  reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.

back_blocks.md: A reaction that goes to completion uses up all the **reactants** and stops, whereas a **reversible** reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.

front_blocks.md: Define **Le Chatelier's principle**.

back_blocks.md: **Le Chatelier's principle** states that if a change is made to a system at dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to minimise that change.

cards.front_md: Define **Le Chatelier's principle**.
cards.back_md: **Le Chatelier's principle** states that if a change is made to a system at dynamic equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to minimise that change.

front_blocks.md: What happens to the position of equilibrium when the concentration of a reactant is increased?

back_blocks.md: The position of equilibrium shifts to the **right**, towards the products, to reduce the increased concentration of the reactant.

cards.front_md: What happens to the position of equilibrium when the concentration of a reactant is increased?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with the greater number of gas molecules.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with the **fewer** gas molecules, to reduce the pressure.

front_blocks.md: If the temperature of an equilibrium is increased, the position of equilibrium shifts in the **..........**  direction to absorb the extra energy.

back_blocks.md: If the temperature of an equilibrium is increased, the position of equilibrium shifts in the **endothermic** direction to absorb the extra energy.

front_blocks.md: What effect does a catalyst have on the position of equilibrium?

back_blocks.md: A catalyst has **no effect** on the position of equilibrium. It increases the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the equilibrium position is unchanged.

cards.front_md: What effect does a catalyst have on the position of equilibrium?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Decreasing the temperature of an exothermic reaction shifts the equilibrium to the left.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Decreasing temperature shifts the equilibrium in the **exothermic** direction. For an exothermic forward reaction, this means shifting to the **right**, increasing the yield of products.

front_blocks.md: What effect does adding water to an ionic equilibrium mixture have on the position of equilibrium?

back_blocks.md: Adding water **shifts the equilibrium** towards the side with more particles (Le Chatelier's principle). For a weak acid equilibrium (HA ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> + A<sup>-</sup>), dilution shifts it to the **right**, increasing the **degree of dissociation** even though all ion concentrations fall.

front_blocks.md: For the reaction N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g), what happens to the equilibrium position when pressure is increased?

back_blocks.md: The equilibrium shifts to the **left**, towards N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (g), because there is one mole of gas on the left compared to two on the right, reducing the total number of gas molecules and lowering pressure.

front_blocks.md: Define the **equilibrium constant *****K***<sub>**c**</sub>.

back_blocks.md: An **equilibrium constant** *K*<sub>c</sub> is a value that links the equilibrium concentrations of products and reactants at a given temperature, with each concentration raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient.

front_blocks.md: For the equilibrium aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, write the expression for *K*<sub>c</sub>.

back_blocks.md: *K*<sub>c</sub> = [C]<sup>c</sup> [D]<sup>d</sup> / [A]<sup>a</sup> [B]<sup>b</sup>
Concentrations of **products** appear on the top and **reactants** on the bottom, each raised to the power of their **stoichiometric coefficient**.

front_blocks.md: Define **partial pressure**.

back_blocks.md: A **partial pressure** of a gas in a mixture is the pressure that gas would exert if it occupied the container alone. The total pressure equals the sum of all partial pressures.

front_blocks.md: What is the mole fraction of a gas in a mixture, and what must all mole fractions in a mixture sum to?

back_blocks.md: The **mole fraction** of a gas is the number of moles of that gas divided by the total moles of all gases in the mixture. All mole fractions in a mixture must sum to **1.00**.

back_blocks.md: Concentration (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>) = **number of moles / volume** (dm<sup>3</sup>)
This gives the **equilibrium concentration** needed to substitute into the *K*<sub>c</sub> expression.

front_blocks.md: Define **ICE table**.

back_blocks.md: An **ICE table** (Initial, Change, Equilibrium) is used to organise mole or concentration data, using stoichiometric ratios to find unknown equilibrium values from initial and one equilibrium amount.

front_blocks.md: What are the steps to calculate *K*<sub>p</sub> when only moles of each gas and total pressure are given?

back_blocks.md:
1. Calculate the **total moles** of all gases.
2. Find the **mole fraction** of each gas (moles / total moles).
3. Multiply each mole fraction by the total pressure to get each **partial pressure**.
4. Substitute partial pressures into the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression.

3. Multiply each mole fraction by the total pressure to get each **partial pressure**.
4. Substitute partial pressures into the *K*<sub>p</sub> expression.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
For the reaction H<sub>2</sub> (g) + I<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2HI (g), *K*<sub>p</sub> has units of Pa.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
For this reaction, the total moles of gas on each side are equal (1 + 1 = 2), so all pressure units cancel and *K*<sub>p</sub> is **unitless**.

front_blocks.md: How do you determine the units of *K*<sub>p</sub> after substituting partial pressures into the expression?

back_blocks.md: Write Pa (or kPa) in place of each partial pressure, apply the exponents, then cancel. If more moles of gas appear on top, the units will be Pa raised to a positive power. If more appear on the bottom, the units will be Pa raised to a negative power.

front_blocks.md: For the reaction 2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub> (g), what are the units of *K*<sub>p</sub> if partial pressures are in Pa?

back_blocks.md: *K*<sub>p</sub> = Pa<sup>2</sup> / (Pa<sup>2</sup> x Pa) = **Pa**<sup>**-1**</sup>
There are two moles of gas on top and three on the bottom, so the units simplify to **Pa**<sup>**-1**</sup>.

back_blocks.md: A catalyst speeds up both the **forward and reverse reactions** by the same factor, so the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium is **unchanged** and *K*<sub>c</sub> stays the same.

front_blocks.md: Define **equilibrium position**.

back_blocks.md: An **equilibrium position** is the relative distribution of reactants and products in an equilibrium mixture. It can shift left or right in response to changes in concentration, pressure or temperature.

front_blocks.md: Why is a compromise temperature of 400-450 °C used in the Haber process rather than a lower temperature?

back_blocks.md: The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so lower temperatures would give a higher **equilibrium yield** of NH<sub>3</sub>. However, too low a temperature makes the reaction rate very slow, so **400–450 °C** is a compromise between yield and rate.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The iron catalyst used in the Haber process increases the yield of ammonia at equilibrium.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The iron catalyst increases the **rate** of reaction, allowing equilibrium to be reached faster. It has no effect on the equilibrium position or the yield of ammonia.

front_blocks.md: Why is a pressure of approximately 1 atm used in the Contact process rather than a higher pressure?

back_blocks.md: At low pressures the equilibrium constant *K*<sub>p</sub> for the Contact process is already **very large**, so the yield of SO<sub>3</sub> is **high**. Increasing pressure would add cost with little extra benefit.

The Contact process uses vanadium(V) oxide as its catalyst.

front_blocks.md: How is SO<sub>3</sub> removed from the equilibrium mixture in the Contact process, and why is this done?

back_blocks.md: SO<sub>3</sub> is absorbed into **98% H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> to form **oleum** (H<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>). Removing SO<sub>3</sub> shifts the equilibrium to the right, driving further production of SO<sub>3</sub>.

front_blocks.md: In the Contact process, why is a compromise temperature of about 450 °C used rather than a lower temperature?

back_blocks.md: The reaction is **exothermic**, so lower temperatures favour SO<sub>3</sub> production, but they also reduce the reaction rate. **450 °C** is a compromise that gives an acceptable rate while still achieving a good yield.
